source: Rouder & Ratcliff (2004) Comparing categorization models, J Exp Psychol: General 133:63-82
finding: Four experiments pitted a rule model (general recognition theory) against an exemplar model (GCM) on one-dimensional stimuli with probabilistic category assignment. Rules won when stimuli were confusable. Exemplars won when stimuli were few and distinct.
numbers: 4 experiments; stimuli varied on one axis; assignment probabilities manipulated so the two models made different predictions. No per-model fit values in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only was read (Europe PMC record). Unidimensional stimuli and probabilistic feedback only.
agent_relevance: Strategy depends on stimulus type. Few distinct cases favour case-by-case memory; many confusable cases favour a rule. The S0 gate can route on that: few distinct past problems means retrieve cases, many noisy ones means induce a rule.

source: Rouder & Ratcliff (2006) Comparing exemplar- and rule-based theories of categorization, Curr Dir Psychol Sci 15:9-13
finding: Review of the rule-versus-exemplar literature. Neither theory fits all data. Rules are used with confusable (simple) stimuli, exemplars with distinct (complex) stimuli. They propose a dynamic account: start with rules, learn useful discriminating features, then store stimuli as exemplars.
numbers: No new data. Draws on the 2004 four-experiment series.
limits: Only the abstract page was readable (full text behind a login). The dynamic account is a proposal, not a tested model.
agent_relevance: Suggests a sequence for the agent: try a quick rule first, then keep concrete cases as the problem class becomes familiar. This is a rule-then-exemplar shift, the reverse of the prototype-then-exemplar shift in b04.

source: Nosofsky & Zaki (2002) Exemplar and prototype models revisited: response strategies, selective attention, and stimulus generalization, J Exp Psychol: LMC
finding: Re-analysis of Smith and Minda's prototype-favouring results. The authors say those results confused the type of category representation with the type of response rule (probabilistic vs deterministic). An exemplar model with response scaling fits all of them, and beats prototype models when novel transfer stimuli are tested.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Written by exemplar-theory proponents; Smith and Minda disputed parts of it.
agent_relevance: Warning about measurement: what looks like prototype use can be an artifact of the response rule. Any test of whether the agent uses abstraction or cases must include novel transfer items.

source: Smith & Minda (2000) Thirty categorization results in search of a model, J Exp Psychol: LMC
finding: Re-analysis of 30 uses of the Medin-Schaffer 5-4 category structure across 8 articles over 20 years. The 5-4 structure may encourage exemplar memorising because it is small and poorly structured. Exemplar models only win because they reproduce a training-item advantage. Other models fit as well if given that capacity.
numbers: 30 data sets, 8 articles, 20 years.
limits: Abstract only. Contested by Nosofsky (2000, b05).
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: one small, arbitrary category structure drove a whole field toward exemplar theory. Benchmarks with tiny memorisable item sets will over-reward case memory.

source: Nosofsky (2000) Exemplar representation without generalization? Comment on Smith and Minda's (2000) paper, J Exp Psychol: LMC
finding: Rebuttal of the 30-data-set meta-analysis. Many of the 30 sets did not test the real 5-4 structure, so the model predictions were void. Also argues Smith and Minda's all-or-none exemplar processes in their elaborated prototype models are implausible.
numbers: Argues a subset of the 30 sets is invalid; the abstract gives no count.
limits: Abstract only. Author is the exemplar-model proponent.
agent_relevance: Shows the debate is partly about design validity. Any claim the agent's memory is prototype-like or case-like needs a design that really separates the predictions.

source: Smith & Minda (1998) Prototypes in the mist: the early epochs of category learning, as described in Jagadish et al. (2024)
finding: Task: 14 six-dimensional stimuli, nonlinear category rule, blocks of 56 trials. Human choices were fit better by a prototype model in the early blocks and by an exemplar model in later blocks. This is the classic prototype-to-exemplar shift with practice.
numbers: 14 stimuli, 6 dimensions, block size 56 trials. Humans better fit by prototype for the first five blocks (as reported by Jagadish et al.).
limits: Read second-hand through Jagadish et al.; original paper not opened. Subject to the Nosofsky and Zaki 2002 critique (b03).
agent_relevance: Time course matters: early in a problem class an averaged summary may work; with many cases, retrieval of specific instances takes over. Suggests memory entries should start as summaries and keep raw cases.

source: Jagadish, Coda-Forno, Thalmann, Schulz, Binz (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks, ICML 2024 (arXiv 2402.01821)
finding: A meta-learned network trained on LLM-generated category tasks (ERMI) fit human trial-by-trial choices better than seven cognitive models (RMC, GCM, prototype, Rule, Rulex, plus two meta-learned nets). The classic exemplar, prototype and rule models were each the best explanation for 1 percent or fewer of participants.
numbers: Badham et al. 2017 data, Shepard types 1-4: share of participants best fit by ERMI 0.43 +/- 0.05, RMC 0.41 +/- 0.05, MI 0.10, PFN 0.05; GCM/prototype/Rule/Rulex each at most 0.01.
limits: Human data come from two existing studies. The result is a model comparison on small classic tasks, not a test of an LLM agent. LLM only generated training tasks.
agent_relevance: In this fit, no single pure strategy wins. Human behaviour is a mixture, so the agent should not commit to one memory format.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) CLAUDE-V2 as a direct simulated participant (same paper, Section 5-6, Appendix G-H)
finding: Claude-v2 prompted to learn Shepard-type tasks reached zero error within three blocks on most difficulty levels, but its difficulty ordering did not match humans. It was fully exemplar-based from block 2 on the Smith and Minda task, unlike humans.
numbers: Match to human error rates: Claude MSE 0.18 vs ERMI MSE 0.05. BIC on Badham data: ERMI 38722.13 vs Claude-v2 39816.90. BIC on Devraj data: ERMI 41207.20 vs Claude-v2 42401.42 (lower is better). Claude found type 2 harder than types 3, 4, 5.
limits: One 2023 model (Claude-v2), prompt-based, a paraphrase of participant instructions. Newer models untested.
agent_relevance: A frontier chat LLM learns small category tasks faster than people and leans on exemplar-like lookup, not human-like rule or prototype use. Do not assume human heuristics transfer to the agent.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) ERMI shift from prototype-like to exemplar-like behaviour
finding: ERMI, trained only on LLM-generated tasks, reproduced the human drift toward exemplar-based behaviour over blocks, but earlier: exemplar fit from block 2, where humans took five blocks. Plain meta-learning (MI) without ecological priors showed no such drift.
numbers: ERMI slope of exemplar-minus-prototype error over segments -0.01 +/- 0.004, z=-2.54, p<0.01. MI slope -0.002 +/- 0.005, z=-0.47, p=0.63. Fitted inverse temperature 0.09 +/- 0.01 (ERMI) and 0.17 +/- 0.02 (MI).
limits: Simulated learner, not a language-model agent. Single task family (Smith and Minda).
agent_relevance: Experience with realistic task statistics is what produces the exemplar shift. That backs memory of real past problems over synthetic rules.

source: Xiong, Ji-An, Wilson, Lee, Wei (2026) Large language models reorganize representational geometry during in-context learning, COLM 2026 (arXiv 2605.28854)
finding: Across eight instruction-tuned LLMs, trial-by-trial in-context classification responses were matched best by a prototype (class centroid) learner over final-layer representations. Exemplar, 1-NN, online gradient descent, Bayesian class-mean and Kalman learners matched less well. Successful ICL came with representations becoming more separable.
numbers: Models: Llama3 3B and 8B; Gemma3 1B, 4B, 12B, 27B; Qwen3 4B; Qwen3.5 27B, on ETHICS-commonsense. 200 trials per task condition. Qwen3 4B also tested on five datasets. Agreement figures shown only in a figure, no table value read.
quote: We find that prototype learning best matches the LLM's responses
limits: Descriptive fit only, not proof the LLM runs a prototype algorithm. More flexible linear online learners reached higher accuracy than the prototype learner from the same representations. Tasks are binary and defined on the model's own PCs.
agent_relevance: Gives an LLM-side answer to the human debate: in-context labels get averaged into class centroids. Few-shot examples work like a summary, so choose examples that centre the class.

source: Xiong et al. (2026) limits on what ICL can learn
finding: Tasks were linearly separable by construction yet learnability differed by axis. Axes along the model's leading representation directions were learned fast and well. Axes along trailing components were learned slowly. Boosting activity along the task axis did not improve behaviour.
numbers: Tasks defined by the LR axis and PC1 and similar leading PCs were learned faster than PC32, PC128 and PC512 tasks across the eight models.
limits: Correlational link between geometry and performance; the causal intervention failed to help, so the mechanism is not shown. Effects shown mainly in figures.
agent_relevance: A rule that cuts against how the model already represents things is hard to learn from examples. Rule-induction prompts will fail on categories the model does not already encode; better to supply the rule or decompose.

source: Xu, Zhang, Du, Luo, Qiu, Huang, Zhang (2025) Revealing emergent human-like conceptual representations from language prediction (arXiv 2501.12547)
finding: LLaMA3-70B builds concept representations from a few in-context demonstrations. Using these, prototype-based categorisation of THINGS categories reached 90.64 percent with 24 demonstrations, above FastText and sense vectors. An exemplar-based method gave comparable results.
numbers: Prototype categorisation: LLM 90.64 +/- 0.28 percent (24 demos) vs FastText 77.86 and sense vectors 85.13. Similarity ratings: rho 0.776 +/- 0.007 at 72 demos vs FastText 0.464, sense vectors 0.513. Odd-one-out: plateau 52.41 +/- 0.31 percent after 48 demos vs FastText 43.49, sense vectors 49.71; human noise ceiling 67.67 +/- 1.08.
limits: Concept-level (words), not trial-and-error learning of new categories. LLM struggled where humans used colour or texture.
agent_relevance: Prototype and exemplar readouts perform about the same on familiar word categories, so the choice of memory format matters little there. It will matter on novel or odd categories.

source: Russin, Pavlick, Frank (2025) The dynamic interplay between in-context and in-weight learning in humans and neural networks (arXiv 2402.08674v5)
finding: In humans, blocked training beats interleaved when categories follow a simple rule, and interleaved beats blocked when no succinct rule exists (task x curriculum interaction). A meta-learned network with in-context learning shows the blocking advantage on rule-like tasks. A network with only in-weight learning shows an interleaving advantage in both conditions.
numbers: Human interaction p=0.04; blocking advantage d=0.47 for rule-like categories; interleaving advantage d=0.33 for rotated (non-rule) categories. Stimuli: two features with 8 values each, 64 items, two categories. Model: ICL main effect of rotation p<10^-3, of curriculum p<0.05.
limits: Human numbers quoted from an earlier human study, not re-run. The ICL network is a small metalearned model, not a pretrained LLM. Retention is worse with ICL.
agent_relevance: Order of examples should depend on whether a rule exists: group by class when a rule is likely; mix when not. Supports a rule-present check before ordering memory-retrieved cases.

source: Lewandowsky (2011) Working memory capacity and categorization: individual differences and modeling, J Exp Psychol: LMC
finding: Working memory capacity predicted learning of all six Shepard, Hovland and Jenkins problem types. One latent variable covered performance on all six. A single latent variable also captured variation in ALCOVE learning parameters across problems.
numbers: N = 113; six problem types; structural equation modelling; ALCOVE fit per participant.
limits: Abstract only. Correlational. One shared factor means WMC does not separate rule from exemplar learners.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in working memory show up in both rule and similarity tasks. For an agent, context length or scratch-space budget is a general limit, not specific to one strategy (links to the working memory subfield).

source: Hoffmann, von Helversen, Rieskamp (2014) Pillars of judgment: how memory abilities affect performance in rule-based and exemplar-based judgments, J Exp Psychol: General
finding: People switched strategy between rule-based and exemplar-based judgment tasks. Working memory predicted success on rule-based tasks. Episodic memory predicted accuracy on the exemplar-based task. Choosing an exemplar strategy was linked to better episodic memory, but working memory was unrelated to which strategy was chosen.
numbers: N = 279 participants. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract page only. Judgment (continuous) tasks, not category labels.
agent_relevance: Two different resources limit the two strategies: working memory for rules, stored-case recall for exemplars. An agent has analogues (reasoning budget vs retrieval quality). Match the weaker resource to the strategy.

source: Badham, Sanborn, Maylor (2017) Deficits in category learning in older adults: rule-based versus clustering accounts, Psychol Aging
finding: Young and older adults learned classic Shepard-type problems to test three accounts: older adults struggle with complex rules, with using rules at all, or with clustering by similarity. This age moderator is the data set later used by Jagadish et al.
numbers: Abstract truncated in the record; no figures read.
limits: Abstract only and cut off. Outcome of the three-way contrast not read.
agent_relevance: Shows that rule use and similarity use can be separated by individual differences, so a single average strategy is misleading.

source: Lee & Vanpaemel (2008) Exemplars, prototypes, similarities and rules in category representation: an example of hierarchical Bayesian analysis, Cognitive Science
finding: A hierarchical Bayesian version of the Varying Abstraction Model fit 30 published Nosofsky-lab data sets. Representations ran from pure exemplar through partial merging to pure prototype. Some data sets gave a split posterior with real mass on both extremes. Rule-instruction groups merged stimuli (abstraction, low weight on similarity); free-learning groups used exemplars.
numbers: 30 previously published data sets from six Nosofsky-lab papers; 14 shown in the main figure. In Fig 6 for data sets 11 and 15 posterior mass for top representations was 0.36, 0.20, 0.12, 0.10 and 0.39, 0.36, 0.13. Participants per set ranged from about 28 to 164 in the table.
limits: All data from one lab and one stimulus family (Shepard circles, shape and brightness, pitch and line length). Stimuli with little to merge give exemplar fits by default.
agent_relevance: Instructions changed the representation: telling people a rule moved them from exemplars to merged, rule-like categories. Prompting with a stated rule could do the same for the agent.

source: Lee & Vanpaemel (2008), representational change over time
finding: Across beginning, middle and end blocks of two tasks, abstraction decreased with learning: representations moved toward pure or near-pure exemplar. This agrees with the Smith-Minda and Johansen-Palmeri shift, though only suggestively.
numbers: Data sets 25-27 and 28-30 (table lists 164 and 120 in the participants column, reading uncertain) from Nosofsky and Palmeri 1998.
limits: The authors call the evidence suggestive. Two task pairs only.
agent_relevance: A second, independent analysis pointing the same direction as b06: practice shifts toward stored cases.

source: Nosofsky, Palmeri, McKinley (1994) Rule-plus-exception model of classification learning, Psychol Review 101
finding: RULEX: people form simple logical rules and memorise occasional exceptions. Learning is stochastic, so individuals differ widely and averaged data blend idiosyncratic rules and exceptions. Accounts for prototype and exemplar effects, sensitivity to correlated features, and harder learning of non-linearly-separable sets.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Later work (b07) found RULEX the best explanation for 1 percent or fewer of participants on Shepard types 1-4.
agent_relevance: The hybrid pattern, a rule plus a short list of exceptions, is a candidate memory format for problem classes: rule first, exceptions stored as cases.

source: Goodman, Tenenbaum, Feldman, Griffiths (2008) A rational analysis of rule-based concept learning, Cognitive Science 32:108-154
finding: Rational Rules model: Bayesian inference over a grammar of logical rules. It matched human generalisation judgments in several well-known category experiments, for averages and for individuals. It also explained judgments on a broader set of 7-feature concepts.
numbers: No correlations read; abstract (via Europe PMC) gives none.
limits: Abstract only; full text could not be opened (PDF host returned error). Fit quality here comes from the authors' own model.
agent_relevance: Rules preferred by simplicity (short logical descriptions) look human-like. Supports a bias to the shortest rule that fits the stored cases.

source: Fific, Little, Nosofsky (2010) Logical-rule models of classification response times, Psychol Review 117:309-348
finding: Logical-rule models, which combine independent per-dimension random-walk decisions through logical rules, were tested against exemplar-based random walk (EBRW) and a distance-from-boundary model on response times. In Experiment 1 the rule models fit much better; the EBRW and coactive models wrongly predicted over-additive mean RT patterns and faster interior than exterior stimuli.
numbers: Fit by BIC; nine stimuli with six correct and six error RT quantiles each (99 degrees of freedom per subject). Small-N, individual-subject design (two speed subjects in Experiment 2).
limits: Authors chose conditions maximally favourable to rules ('validation testing') and still say rule models did not give complete accounts. They explicitly do not claim rule use is common. Few participants.
agent_relevance: Response times can tell rules from exemplars when choices cannot. A latency or token-count signature could be used to detect rule versus lookup in the agent.

source: Ashby & Rosedahl (2017) A neural interpretation of exemplar theory, Psychol Review 124:472-482
finding: A striatal-learning neural model is mathematically equivalent to the GCM under five assumptions, and nearly so with them relaxed. Because the accounts predict nearly the same behaviour, goodness of fit cannot tell them apart. Behavioural dissociations between rule-based and information-integration learning are what separate them.
numbers: R-squared of neural model vs GCM across four category structures: .999, .999, .981, .990. Relaxed model vs exemplar-equivalent: .999, .998, .981, .955. Simulation conditions 1,200 training and 3,500 transfer trials. At least 25 empirical RB vs II dissociations. II learning is best with 500 ms feedback delay, delays of 2.5 s or longer abolish most II learning, while delays up to 10 s do not affect RB learning.
limits: Simulation, no human data. Equivalence is asymptotic only and does not cover early learning. Evidence for medial temporal involvement is mixed (three amnesia studies found deficits, many found none).
agent_relevance: Model mimicry: fit alone cannot decide rule vs exemplar. Use manipulations (feedback delay, dual task, instruction) that dissociate the systems, as the agent's evaluation should.

source: Lian & Varma (2024) Cobweb as a unifying model of exemplar and prototype learning (arXiv 2403.03835)
finding: A hierarchical concept-learning system (Cobweb) shows prototype-like or exemplar-like predictions depending on the node it uses, and reproduces classic Medin-Schaffer and Shepard-replication patterns. It need not fit one pure type.
numbers: Only qualitative findings read; no fit values extracted.
limits: Skimmed, not read in detail; only partial text checked by search. Not a human-data replication.
agent_relevance: A tree of concepts at several levels of abstraction is one way to store both summaries and cases; query the level that fits the data volume.

source: Shepard, Hovland, Jenkins (1961) Learning and memorization of classifications, Psychol Monographs 75(13)
finding: Six types of two-category splits of eight stimuli. Type I (one-dimension rule) is learned fastest, Type VI (no rule) slowest, with Type II (XOR-like) easier than Types III-V under the usual finding.
numbers: From memory of the standard result; not verified this session. Jagadish et al. report that Nosofsky et al. (1994) replicated the order and that Claude-v2 found type 2 harder than 3-5 (b08).
limits: Not opened. The Type II advantage is what pure similarity models (unattended GCM) have trouble with; attention weights fix it.
agent_relevance: Difficulty ordering is a ready test to see if the agent learns categories like humans (it did not in b08).

source: Medin & Schaffer (1978) Context theory of classification learning, Psychol Review 85
finding: Introduced the context (exemplar) model and the 5-4 category structure. Source of the structure analysed in Smith and Minda 2000 (b04) and Nosofsky 2000 (b05).
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Second-hand only (via the b04, b05 abstracts and Cobweb text).
agent_relevance: Origin of the benchmark that drove the exemplar debate; reminder to check structure validity (b04).

source: Kruschke (1992) ALCOVE: an exemplar-based connectionist model of category learning, Psychol Review 99
finding: Exemplar network with learned attention to dimensions. Used in Lewandowsky 2011 (b14) to fit all six Shepard problems with shared learning parameters.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Known only through the b14 abstract.
agent_relevance: Attention learning is the piece that lets exemplar models explain rule-like ordering; an agent analogue is learning which features of a problem to attend to.

source: Johansen & Palmeri (2002) Are there representational shifts during category learning?, Cognitive Psychology 45
finding: Studied transfer to novel stimuli across training and reported a shift from rule-based to exemplar-based responding with experience (cited by Rouder & Ratcliff 2006, Fific et al. 2010, and used by Jagadish et al. for a 9-stimulus, 4-dimension transfer test with items T1-T7).
numbers: From Jagadish et al.: nine four-dimensional training stimuli, seven transfer stimuli T1-T7. Other numbers not read.
limits: Not opened. Claims about the shift direction come from citing papers (b02, b21).
agent_relevance: Transfer items are the discriminating test: rules and exemplars predict different generalisation to unseen cases.

source: Gap note: direct LLM tests of Shepard six types, 5-4 structure or RULEX/GCM fits (2020-2026)
finding: arXiv keyword searches for Shepard types or exemplar/prototype/rule with language models returned almost nothing beyond Jagadish 2024, Xiong 2026, Xu 2025 and Russin 2025. A Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex search was blocked by rate limits. So the LLM literature found here is thin and mostly about in-context learning geometry, not classic category-structure benchmarks.
numbers: Four arXiv queries run; one relevant hit (2402.01821); web search added 2605.28854, 2501.12547, 2402.08674, 2403.03835.
limits: Search coverage is partial because of API blocks; absence of results is not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: A direct Shepard-types test on current frontier models appears to be an open experiment we could run cheaply on our own agent.
